purpose: Cefaclor is an antibiotic used to fight bacterial infections. It is commonly prescribed for ear infections, throat infections like strep throat, sinus infections, urinary tract infections, and certain skin or chest infections. It only works against bacteria — it will not help with colds, the flu, or other viral illnesses.
how_it_works: Cefaclor works by attacking the outer shell, called the cell wall, of harmful bacteria. Without this protective wall, the bacteria fall apart and die. Think of it like dissolving the armor that protects the bacteria, so your body can clear the infection.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include upset stomach, nausea, diarrhea, and stomach pain. Some people may notice a mild skin rash. Taking it with food can help reduce stomach upset. These effects are usually mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to penicillin antibiotics, because there is a small chance you could also react to cefaclor. Stop taking it right away and seek medical help if you develop a severe rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing — these could be signs of a serious allergic reaction. Also let your doctor know if you get severe or persistent diarrhea, as it could signal a serious gut infection. Always finish the full course of antibiotics even if you feel better early, to make sure the infection is fully cleared.
typical_dosing: For adults, the usual dose is 250 mg to 500 mg taken by mouth every 8 hours (three times a day). For children, the dose is based on body weight and is determined by the doctor. It can be taken with or without food, but food may help reduce stomach upset. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and complete the entire prescribed course.
